en: Kṣemendra: *Narmamālā*, the first jest:
By whom this entire world has been deluded through his own will by means of illusion—
Victorious is that glorious Kāyastha, the unconquered Supreme Lord.
There is the land of Kaśmīra, the foremost among those possessing well-being, adorned by circles of wise men, which has shattered the pride of Indra’s abode.

In that city dwelt King Ananta, the conqueror of Bali, who was resplendent like the glorious Trivikrama when the prowess of his enemies was paralyzed by the pillar-like strength of his arms, which consumed abundant offerings.
When that discerning king had thus warded off calamities for the people and reduced the wicked officials to nothing but memory, [he ruled]. (KN 1.4)
A certain connoisseur was addressed by a certain man, who was an ornament to the crest of the learned, who excelled in playful wit,
and who was the most eminent in assemblies of scholars.
Urged to perform a deed that transcends the conduct of one who has passed beyond laughter, he engages in a mockery of misconduct through that very occasion.
Homage to the creator of the manifold world, the master of illusion,
the agent of its origination, maintenance, and destruction, the destroyer of the cities [of the demons].
To you, the all-pervading, who are devoid of birth, beyond qualities, yet possessing the creative arts;
to you, the sovereign of all, the consumer of the entire *kālakūṭa* poison.
Long ago, when the Daityas had been slain by the powerful Viṣṇu,
the lord of their household became sorrowful and filled with long-standing world-weariness.
Having gone to the banks of the Vaitaraṇī, he performed austerities for a thousand years,
subsisting on handfuls of his own urine due to his enmity toward the gods.
Satisfied, Kali, the giver of boons, approached him in person and said:
"Go, my child, to the surface of the earth for the destruction of all the gods."
By this Kālamā weapon given by me, which strikes with force,
they shall have their lamps and flowers severed, be deprived of incense, and be left naked.
"You shall make all the gods dwell in ruined abodes, smeared with dust, crying out 'Alas! Alas!', surrounded by dogs, and longing for food and water."
If you were to cut off the livelihood of the Brahmins in this world,
the gods in heaven would undoubtedly perish due to the cessation of sacrifices.
"Since you wept in heaven when the destruction of the Daityas was accomplished,
therefore you shall become famous on earth by the name Divira."
For one who has always subdued all illusion (sakalamāya), the Goddess Kālī— who has swallowed up every illusion (māyā)— bestows the accomplishment of all goals.
In your lineage here, there will arise Daityas in the form of ministers,
by whom this earth— once its power has been seized— will no longer exist.
When he had spoken thus and vanished, that man of defiled mind,
as time passed through its vast expanse, descended to the earth.
Then he was born on the earth from a butcher who struck his vital organs,
the son of the wife of a digger, and one whose vow was to uproot the world.
Born into that lineage were those who were fierce, who destroyed all means of livelihood, who were harsh,
who had no friends, who were wicked, and who plundered everything.
As if at the end of an eon, with all moving and stationary beings everywhere swallowed up,
they were like those whose entire bodies were smeared with ink, as if embraced by Time itself.
With those parts of the body that move downward, those that are soft, those that are rigid, and those that suddenly protrude—
just like excrement residing within the body— these bodily constituents cause various afflictions.
During the time of service, he was surrounded by many-faced hunters with many arms,
by enemies of the gods who were skilled in deception, possessed of many illusions, and assuming many forms.
At that time, while the lands of cities, villages, towns, and market-towns were pervaded [by darkness], he scratched the sky with a pen smeared with ink.
"With a dagger in his hand, clad in birch-bark,
and wearing a bellows as a sash— this great Asura, a devourer of all,
has been born for the destruction of the world! so sang the throngs of Piśācas.
By that *divira*, who steals the gods' [offerings], who slaughters cows, and who is a thief of salt,
much is consumed and drunk day and night.
In ancient times, during the Lord Viṣṇu’s conquest of the three worlds,
Dharma fled out of devotion [to him] and remains in the form of liquid ink.

For that Lord who dwells within the body, who cuts through the constant, occasional, and occasional-omitted [impurities] of gods, nāgas, and humans, there is once again the conquest of the three worlds.
The Kali age has departed; it remains in the form of flowing ink.
Just as the Gaṅgā bestows heaven, so too does this [ink] lead to hell.
Distressed by notorious villages, shackles, and likewise by clubs,
he attained a state of world-weariness out of fear and became one who observes the great vow.
Then, his pain broken, he abandoned his vow and departed for another region;
after some time, having been forgotten, Bhūrja returned, feigning a lack of desire.

In due course, by virtue of his appointment to a village, he reached the position of a village accountant in the city; there, though esteemed for his hypocrisy, he obtained the management of household affairs through the power of destiny.
By his cruel dependents, who lived by following his lead,
the earth was stripped of its wealth by those who were manifest thieves.
Dambhadhvaja, Niṣprapañca, Lubdhaka, Kalamākara, Sūcīmukha, Bhūrjagupta, and Mahīmaṇḍa were difficult to withstand.
"These seven incarnations of the Daityas are officials by virtue of their own greatness;
they are all to be plundered, executed, and worshipped," they said in their arrogance.
Upatāpa, Vajrapāta, Parigha the breaker of doors,
Dhūmaketu, Kapimukha, Kukṣibheda, and Gṛholmuka.
These eight piśācas were his chief warriors and precursors;
with staffs in their hands, they roamed about for the destruction of the world of mortals.
Surrounded by hundreds of servants, he would always recite a hymn during the worship of Dambhahara, crying out "Alas! Alas! with tears in his eyes.
"Yesterday, while she was looking on with her sweet, heart-stealing voice,
how many of my patients were treated by me at Vijayeśvara?"
Victorious is the Supreme Lord, whose infinite majesty has been made manifest!
May these seventy-three [treatises] proceed above those that existed from the beginning.

May those Bhaṭṭas who have mostly died in their own homes be dragged about by fetters around their ankles— those who were once flourishing with the wealth of prosperity, compassion, awakening, and supreme bliss!
May that unconquered one, whose majesty is illuminated by knowledge, be victorious;
may the officials who produce smoke without fire go to the villages!
To him whose nature is universal bliss and who is the cause of all auspiciousness,
they were sentenced to death after having been stripped of all their possessions, for they had obstructed the administration of justice.
Salutations to the Brahman whose nature is consciousness, the remover of all afflictions;
when oppressed, living beings surely flow forth like drops from guggulu seeds.
Thus, resonant with such hymns of praise and deafening all with the sound of his bell, he gave his command and quickly entered the assembly hall crowded with officials.
Marīci, established in his renowned abode, beheld from afar an official messenger approaching on business, brought there by the misdeeds of the people.
It was a device for the expulsion of gods from temples, featuring a wheel that brought misfortune to those standing beneath its feet,
with a sharp point raised by the precise division of the arrangement of extremely fine blades.
It had the hue of an *atasī* flower, its soft touch was like that of a protective amulet,
and it was wrapped in a thick cotton cloth fragrant with the scent of genuine musk.
With a golden rosary of triple-stranded beads resting upon his fingers,
he was making distorted movements with his mouth due to the heavy breathing caused by the fatigue of the long journey.
Seeing Piśuna approaching nearby,
that devotee of the Lord rose up with joy, took him by the hand, and seated him at his side.
Thus ends the section on the Lord of Domestic Affairs.
Homage to those informers by whose favor officials,
even when situated at a distance, become possessed of thousands of ears and eyes.
He said: "Having heard that you were standing at the forefront of the powerful, I have come from the temple, acting as a guide for the path to this heap."
Whatever garments, ornaments, jewels, and so forth exist in the temples of the gods—
all of that without exception, I shall make manifest to you.
At Vijayeśvara, Vārāha, Mārtaṇḍa, and other such places,
there exists a multitude of shrines that, through the accumulation of your good fortune, will fulfill the needs of those you support.
Fearless toward slanders and unhesitating regarding sins,
let a harsh man be appointed there as a constant and thorough protector.
And there exists on earth a famous scribe equal to you,
who— without wealth, without effort, and without seizing all one's possessions— [performs his work].
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are not even counted, let alone the killing of cows,
by that person who uproots the populace through devotion to his master.
There are others everywhere as well, but one such as he is not to be found:
the wealthy man who brought his own father to his death while in prison.
If indeed he should come to you through my word because of your merits,
then know his own home to be a palace at his own command, filled with treasures.
To him who was speaking thus repeatedly, having made a secret agreement with his ear, Mahattama said: "Let him be brought here quickly."
Then, having ascertained that the protector was a sinner, he quickly had him brought there after two or three respectful round-trips.
Thus spoke the wheelwright or the libertine,
his neck stiff and held high like a wooden post, his eyes motionless and turned upward,
wearing a turban and tunic that had the yellowish-green hue of jaundice.
He was possessed by a vast, hanging belly that resembled a foul-smelling cave and appeared like a cavernous house of flesh.
Intense arrogance, great wrath, life-destroying and incurable,
accompanied by calamities and torments— like a fever caused by the derangement of the humors (sannipāta).
Having encountered a great and unbearable gadfly,
he subdued it with ease and obtained many temples.
Then, surrounded by countless attendants who seemed like personified efforts moving before him, he suddenly went to offer the water of honor (*argha*).
People perceived that this Hiraṇyākṣa was a mere glass trinket, having come to destroy the gods while recollecting his former enmity.
When the creditors had fled from the temple out of fear,
those who resided in the temple returned there once more, their wealth undiminished.
While the soldiers, frantic with the task of bursting open the bolted doors and panels, had begun the great festival of plundering the household vessels and other goods; ||| KNarm_1.69 |||
There arose the piteous sound of weeping from the housewives whose clothes had been suddenly snatched away, and from their terrified children.
Thus spoke the protector.
Then there arrived one who had come after a long time, his gait faltering with great joy;
he was emaciated, slow-moving like Saturn, grey, and his belly was ravaged by hunger.
His head was covered by a tattered turban with many holes,
and his body armor was stitched together from hundreds of leather patches and smeared with dirt.
With the hem of his garment tucked into a waistband made of tattered, worn-out rags,
the wretch was tormented by the pain of his feet in the dried-out footwear he had obtained through begging.
The scribe, though destitute, is proud of his skill in drafting documents;
when commanded by the steward, he is like a serpent subsisting on air.
His wife had her waist covered with a tattered fragment of cloth;
the tip of her nose was smeared with collyrium, and she wore earrings of dangling clay.
Angry because her child was hungry, with half a winnowing basket covering her head,
she stood up with a hissing sound and repeatedly scratched her buttocks.
When her husband had finally attained his position, she was filled with joy;
gathering from here and there, she worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas with offerings of betel-nut, cakes, incense, and other gifts.
Having attentively heard the messages concerning many matters from his lord, he,
with hands outstretched to receive payment, wrote the letters without error.
Like a monkey struck by a stone, his voice raised with the shrill cries of running pigeons,
he quickly gave two hundred letters while counting out dinars.
Whatever is required for the feet of those who protect [the world]—
whether it be a ladle, a grass mat, a cloth pouch, or a vessel, bowl, and casket— [is provided].
By granting such letters and the like, he attained supreme renown;
before long, he became robust, his hands full of wealth, and arrogant with pride.
Reading the letters of the documents with blurred vision,
he made various contortions by knitting his eyebrows and squinting his eyes.
Thus says the scribe Upādhyāya. Then, having accepted the arrangement regarding the breaking of the parasol of the mediator, the Gañja-divira arrived, requested by Bhaṭṭa Bhāgavata.
Proud because of his frequent humiliations, he had discarded his tattered rags;
the half of his forehead was whitened by the cloth wound around his head.
Intent on the destruction of all temples, villages, and constellations,
he left nothing remaining of the guardians of the gods except for their ropes.
Having obtained it, he granted a long period of six months,
within which four hundred thousand verses were written.
Then, questioned by him with a gesture of acceptance regarding the means for his own purpose, he—
who was established in a state of goodness— spoke somewhat out of contentment with his lot.
In this temple, those various renowned guardians,
having sold all their own possessions, have departed as my adversaries.
But today, out of affection, I must perform a service for you;
for that Blessed One is the family preceptor and the sole guru of us both.
In this world, having accepted five or six wheel-turning Śivas through the practice of giving,
they enjoy all the property of the gods as well as the status of a personal attendant.
Whatever remains from what was sold exists within the circle of the gods; all that is enjoyed by you as if it were your own, solely through his consent.
For instance, previously I brought a large copper pot;
out of devotion, I fashioned a bell for the temple from a hundredth part of it.
Having sold the bell at the proper time, he made a water-pot from a portion of the proceeds;
that too was gradually eaten away, and with what remained, he made a small bell.
Having thus for a long time crushed even that fine *jhilīmālī* flower into powder, he then preserved a small portion of the bell-metal (*ghaṇṭā*) fragment.
"In this way, a four-armed plunder is carried out through the worship of Śiva;
there are thousands of grains of rice here, so let them be used by you.
Therefore, I shall request of you one named Krayavikrayika."
Thus, by means of those various hundreds of stratagems described [by him],
that protector rendered the abode of the gods empty, like a man with worn-out hooves cracking a walnut.
Thus spoke Gañjadivira.
Then Pravīṇa, who was intent on other heaps and skilled at plundering the virtuous,
being knowledgeable in his duty, departed from that village to quell the calamity.
In the interior of that Great Raurava hell, which was covered with refuse,
there was a great vessel for holding water whose spout was broken and cracked.
In whose house there once dwelt a state of existence within the hollow of a cock's nest, amidst the clattering "khaḍa-khaḍa" sounds of an old door-panel rattling against its fastenings.
With his head wrapped in a piece of burnt felt,
limping slowly with a worn-out, tattered leather sandal that had been gnawed by dogs, he moved along.
Carrying a rag, sesame seeds, clay, *darbha* grass, purificatory rings, and small caskets for the *arghya* offering,
he bore a wooden bowl— once full, now broken and gnawed by mice.
Bathing, his beard bristling from recitation, and established in the path of virtuous conduct,
he would go to the temple of the gods and recite the hymn for half the day.
Performing the circumambulation of cows, bowing before brahmins, and observing the vow of the twelfth day,
he diligently gave even a single cowrie shell to a destitute person on the road.
By the power of fate, the house of that very official, whose business had suddenly arrived,
became filled with household utensils, vessels, and other furnishings.
In the winter, those who did not give him even a charcoal ember were the ones who gave him, unsolicited, whatever clothing and ornaments he desired.
Then his house became white with lime, its courtyards swept clean, filled with many servants, and its inner chambers red with vermilion.
With the fresh luster and beauty born from eating sweet food,
his young wife became in a few days like an apsaras.
As he proceeded from there toward the village, a parasol, a water-pot, and a copper vessel emerged ahead of him, along with his basket, bedding, and other belongings.
A spear, a water-vessel, a bell, a copper bowl, sandals,
a small knife, the feet of the Blessed One, a birch-bark bag, and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
A rosary, an inkwell, a mirror, a bathing cloth,
a casket, a small box, swords, sandals, and a manuscript of mantras.
An astrological chart, a sword-blade, a red woolen blanket,
a sacred thread, a lute-string, a needle, a rice-ear, and a pair of scissors.
Vaca root, a protective amulet made of lac, a small knife, a meditation belt,
hymns and mantras, clay from the Gaṅgā, bilva fruit, and a plowshare smeared with food remnants.
Having gathered together all the household utensils and furnishings brought here and there with the intention of never giving them away again, she went before him.
With his hand raised high toward the creeper, having hired a horse for hire,
he struck it with his heel with a *jhāṅ* sound, while repeatedly leaning his face forward.
As if threatening the people with his gaze, making them as if ablaze,
he went through the city with loose, thick garments, leaping about.
Then he entered the village, wearing a well-washed white cloth,
like an old crane arrived for the destruction of the village fish.
Then, under the pretext of various practices such as eating, thousands of treasures came before him, just like those of the Lord of Yakṣas.
The yogi is intent on the thought of abduction; the one who strives for union is joined to birch bark; the one separated from his wife is an enjoyer of the riches of hell. (KN 1.118)
Useless for the production of fruit, yet solely intent on manifesting faults, the Ashoka tree is a constant source of disease; may the Sovereign, however, be ever victorious!
When thousands of trees had been climbed and hundreds of men were nearly exhausted,
his village was ruined, becoming like a hellish realm.
What need is there to mention his treatment toward men who have committed every offense, when he established a prison that serves as the ultimate end for the punishment of cows?
"Confiscation of all property, imprisonment, punishment, and the demolition of the house"—
such terrible words as these constantly fell from his mouth.
About five or six of his servants were constantly burdened like camels,
carrying ghee, honey, silver coins, black pepper, ginger, and rock salt.
Mudga beans, woolen blankets, peacock feathers, sandals, rams, birds,
lotus stalks, grapes, jars of honey, walnuts, couches, and stools.
They carried, without rest, various household utensils such as those made of bell-metal, copper, and iron,
as well as whatever else he commanded by word.
And when he received from his master the written orders for the abandonment of the staff,
he tore them into pieces as small as sesame seeds with his nails, uttering insults and spitting upon them.
While the king’s officer was present, he would constantly eat two *pala* of mung beans with saltless food, consuming meat and ghee only out of hypocrisy.
Thus, the Superintendent of the Road,
having dismissed the Chief Scribe— who was an expert at detecting thefts but unskilled in medicine—
then appointed him as the Superintendent of Waterworks, for he was supremely adept in medical treatment.
Once released from those twelve years of bondage, he— who was skilled in the art of manifesting letters— quickly composed a fraudulent forgery.
Having cut off his own thumb with his left hand, Divīra went in secret to the house of that wicked man and performed the binding of the *bhūrja* leaf.
Taking up the jar of wine between his two knees,
he drank it repeatedly, in measured sips, yet more and more slowly.
With his final finger, he drew a line with a sharp *kalama* pen that produced a high-pitched chirping sound like a cricket, while fondly smearing the letters with saliva.
This was spoken by the illustrious teacher Carmakāra, the lord of the afflicted, who plunders the wealth of Brahmins, gods, and the constant and occasional religious rites.
Repeatedly singing with a harsh voice the cries of one overwhelmed by devotion to Śiva,
he repeatedly picked lice from his woolen blanket and crushed them with the tips of his nails.
Sighing again and again, censuring the activities of worldly existence,
and balancing his expenditures with his income, he was filled with joy.
Like a possessed vampire reeling from intoxication, he trembled,
encircled by a garland of skeletons mixed with rising clouds of dust.
He was filled with the delight of loud musical instruments emitting the crackling sound of "phaṭ" from thick birch-bark;
his two testicles were dangling out through the holes of a skull-drum.
With his body smeared by the mass of ink-pots rolling about,
the drunken scribe danced naked, having broken both his mat and his water-jar.
Gray and with limbs smeared with filth, he rose up like a piśāca;
filled with intoxication, he rejoiced in the taking of people's lives.

For a long time in that secluded place, he experienced an indescribable delight in the music of his shoulders, accompanied by the clanging sounds produced by the friction of his armpits as he rubbed them together.
Thus did the village clerk;
though constantly occupied by that plundering clerk,
the forest of Janaka blazed up along with him, like a fire with the wind.
Then, not long after his house had become immensely wealthy,
Mālyavatī, adorned with ornaments and observing a vow of chewing betel leaves, [prepared herself].
The housewife, intent on her mirror and looking out toward the royal highway,
bore the pride of the king's other women who were separated from him.
"The necklace is a burden; the golden earring is not dear to me. Fie on this heavy golden thread, fit only for the wives of merchants!"
"Only this single string of pearls is lovely; this is my beloved Lalitā"—at these words of pride, who was not struck with wonder?
Oh, what an ink! It bestows the accomplishment of all tasks.
Oh, what an extraordinary pen! It rests upon the lotus and is exceedingly powerful.
She who drank the raw rice-gruel begged for her when it was served in a broken, stitched stone bowl—
by that very same woman is now drunk camphor-honey from a silver vessel.
Having thus observed the beautiful Kāyastha woman from below in her palace, the noble women who were daughters of her neighbors spoke as follows:
Thus ends the first jest in the *Narmamālā*.
The second jest: That fawn-eyed girl, as if being split apart by the pride of her agitating youth,
did not even look at the earth.
She was at odds with her mother-in-law; she was a young neighborly girl, fond of humorous conversation, and devoted to song and instrumental music.
Her limbs anointed with lovely fragrance, she did not take up her bodice,
revealing the fullness of her breasts as her upper garment slipped halfway down.
Yawning, she turned around and, with her eyes cast askance,
the tremulous-eyed woman gazed at the people, her creeper-like triple-fold of skin gracefully twisting.
Seeing that lovely-eyed woman who could be won without effort, libertines wandered about near her house, coming and going with no other occupation.
For a long time, those seeking that [wealth] were adorned with variegated garments and ornaments,
and they spent their money on fragrant oils, betel, incense, and the like.
Their hopes were fixed upon the wealth of the official, and they were eager for the acquisition of that jewel of a woman;
they displayed hundreds of gestures such as smiles and the twinkling of eyes.
Those serpents, who move with playful crookedness, remain unrecognized even by those who know them; they watch for vulnerabilities and long to sting.
Having gone to an empty temple, two or three notorious adulterers consulted with their neighbors regarding a means to have intercourse with her.
There, one rake said: "She is easily obtained, there is no doubt;
how can she endure her own husband, who is bald, pot-bellied, and old?"
One who is a constant traveler, greedy, envious, incapable of sexual pleasure,
smelling like the scent of a rutting goat, a heavy spitter, and deceitful.
Her son’s death was not a hindrance to this barren woman, nor was there any decline in her vitality;
she was neither overwhelmed by grief nor seen to be consumed by passion.
"Indeed, even women of immoral character do not come [to such a state] because of these faults.
Another said: "You have reflected with a hidden intention;
however, one must exert effort in becoming familiar through close proximity."
Without marriage ceremonies, sacrifices, pilgrimages, and festivals for the gods,
one cannot gain access to the wives of others.
Gazing for a very long time, repeatedly tossing about her curling locks,
engaging in conversations connected to him under some pretext, and manifesting a desire for renunciation.
The manifestation of success in enjoyments, good fortune, and fame;
speech that is very soft and spontaneous; and attentiveness in listening to her words.
His eyes were fixed upon her face as she kissed and embraced the child,
while she was observed adorning him with garments and ornaments.
Once intimacy has been established, there is the offering of garlands, betel, and the like;
pressing firmly against the wall, and kissing in a secluded place.
Secret touching and sexual pleasure—these are the means for the destruction of moral conduct;
in this way, what woman indeed has not been made by me averse to virtue?
"The wife of an official is always available and eager for union;
thus, one who approaches another's wife [is a transgressor].
Then the third also said, "Everything is indeed under our own control."
However, in this case, an obstacle is observed due to the aversion toward the prescribed rule.
This very one, who acts as Citragupta in the department of the sharp-eyed [judges], who inflicts every terror upon living beings, and who is the destroyer of the Nirguṭas; ||| KNarm_2.21 |||
By means of such stratagems as removing loads, breaking chains, and providing false documents,
he caused the *nirguṭas* to be reduced to the state of cowherds and shepherds.
If this [Death] is indeed Time, then why does it take away the lives of men?
If it is the fortnights, then why is it the destroyer of only one woman?
"Who has died today? Where?"—asking this again and again, this one who lives on the dead is equal to a dog; he observes the vow of a Kāpālika.
With his hand raised to seize even those who abide in the conduct of the virtuous,
he offers us a handful of sesame seeds for hell— a gift accompanied by faults.
Although he was a lover of his daughter-in-law and a brilliant member of the family of wine-sellers,
nevertheless, everyone is all-knowing when it comes to observing the faults of others.
Alternatively, I do indeed have a friend who is powerful and a favorite of the king;
by his mere word alone, he will protect all our lives.
House-burners, those who kill cows, women, children, or Brahmins—
many such people were protected by him, even though they served him merely as rumors heard from all quarters.
Thus speaks Jīvanadivira:
"The wife of the official enters her house with excessive boldness;
she is a perpetual female mendicant, a procuress, and a Vajrayoginī."
She who is the mother of those who have mastered the yogas and of paramours, the accomplished messenger (*siddhadūtī*),
is the deity of the pledge (*samayadevatā*) for women during the initiations for rebirth as men.
That ancient harlot indeed deceives even Arundhatī with ease; for she regards the Ganges as a mere blade of grass.
"She will accomplish our desire before long," said those rogues, and they went to the house of the elderly female ascetic.
O female ascetic, once, while his limbs were filled with the food from the alms-hall and his youth had returned, he came again to that very same palace to see the fawn-eyed woman.
He bore a broad tilaka mark made of burnt sandalwood, wore a massive mass of matted hair,
and was arrogant with the loud, resonant sound of his peacock-feather sandals.
With his lower garment tucked between his thighs and not even touching the Brahmins, he rebuked the people in a fit of anger, shouting, "Hey there! You son of a slave woman! and so forth.
Carrying a lotus leaf, the foolish teacher of the monastery was suddenly overcome with astonishment,
as if bitten by the god of love.
Approaching the teacher of the children in the householder's home,
he came daily as a tutor for the sake of learning the alphabet, receiving his monthly fee.
Having gained entry, that rogue, meditating on her alone, recited his lesson;
although he knew all the scripts, he slowly wrote only the syllable *oṃ*.
Surrounded by the women of the house out of curiosity, he stood facing him;
the teacher, for his part, remained there mentally counting the dinars.
Thinking, "I shall teach the *Aṣṭāvatārastotra*," he became exceedingly arrogant, as if he were omniscient himself.
May the feet of the Blessed One protect us— those who are compassionate toward lowly beings,
who destroy the next world [of rebirth], and who ensure safety upon the journey.
Resplendent, moist with saffron, resembling rainbows, marked with the *musimusi* signs, and like mountains of foam;
wearing jewels and gold, anointed with divine perfumes—having entered the fray, may the royal fortune be obtained by us both.
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, between the bilva and the vṛṣabha, and between the two full jars,
there will be a binding of a cloth-strip with five sandalwood marks.
Having given such things as these to the children daily upon wooden platters,
he remained there for a year without fear, calculating his monthly wages.
While performing cutting, writing, sewing with a needle, or applying medicine,
he does not perceive the young boys standing before him.
When addressed as "Preceptor," a musician or a leather-worker, burning with the fire of anger, speaks harshly: "What am I to you? (2.46)

Thus spoke the teacher Dārkopa. As the wife of the official watched the spiritual guide— who was smiling, speaking with smiles, and repeatedly engaging in conversation— she did not move from that spot.
Although he understood the speech uttered by each of those women,
he repeatedly asked with his eyebrows arching in curiosity, "What are you saying?"
Being teased by those intoxicated women with playful jests, mocking insults, and derision, he had a smiling face.
"This man of great fortune knows nothing and understands nothing"—
with this thought, they felt no shame before him, even though they were naked.
Then, though observing the vow of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, he,
being an expert in the pleasures of their company, touched their breasts with his hand.
Like a young stallion released into the herd of mares,
he enjoyed the company of all the women belonging to the official who was away on a journey.
The guide constantly indulged his own will with his brother's wife, his sister, that fawn-eyed woman who was his wife, and others as well.
Having received initiation from that paramour-preceptor, those excellent women became capable of traveling everywhere, established in a vow free from conceptual construction.
Thus spoke the monastery instructor.
Then those rogues, having made their efforts through that female mendicant messenger, enjoyed her— a wanton woman who had come under their control.
Then the eligible man, longing for and remembering his beloved young woman,
quickly entered her [house] wearing clothes filled with [her scent], under the pretext of treating the village for a disease.
For the sake of service, he filled the city with wealthy men carrying loads of ghee, honey, and clarified butter, out of fear.
Having seen him after a long time, she who had observed many suitors perceived him as stout,
rustic, and near to disease, like a vessel filled with water.
And that wife of his, possessing an abundance of mutton, ghee, curd-milk, coagulated milk, and honey,
wept with one eye and laughed with the other.
"This beautiful garment and this ornament have been purchased for you"—
to him who spoke thus, she, being arrogant, made it as if she had heard nothing at all.
That woman, wearing a bandage for anointing her head under the pretext of a headache,
lay moaning beside her husband with a sound.
Then, in that house filled with the tumultuous clamor of a multitude of talkative people and busy village servants, there arose a great festival.
At the end of the day, having consumed much food and being intoxicated by red wine,
the minister lay upon his bed like another Kumbhakarṇa.
Then, at the end of the night, having approached with great difficulty,
his wife was distressed at the embrace and averted her face from the kiss.
Blocking the touch of his hips and rendered motionless by her *ūrūsvastika* posture,
she fell into a sleep quite pointlessly, as if exhausted by her household chores.
Then, when morning had dawned and her birch-bark basket and other belongings were placed before her,
she began to complain of a piercing pain in all her limbs and grew exhausted.
Then, summoned by his attendants, the physician— who was fond of wine and meat—
arrived, considering himself, by fate, to have found a treasure in his hands.
Accompanied by his brothers,
he paid homage to the physician who was devoid of knowledge, a perpetrator of blameworthy acts,
who had destroyed many people like a serpent that brings untimely death.
Confused, he hurried through a hundred houses, panting like one burdened by a heavy load,
repeatedly wiping away the sweat from his forehead with his hand.
Carrying a document containing the names of medicinal herbs and their combinations,
he appeared before the officer of Yama like one who had come from the world of the dead.
He is a physician for wealth and life, yet a non-physician for diseases; he is a lord over one's livelihood, yet afflicted by pain—he by whom people are not abandoned.
Whether he be a physician, or Kālakūṭa poison, or a wild beast, or even a Vetāla,
he who quickly becomes favorable by means of abundant meat is indeed such a one.
That very physician, provoked as the wind that brings about the end of life,
washed away the three impurities with the touch of his hand and destroyed the senses.
What can be said of the physician who performs difficult surgeries on men?
They utter lamentations, saying, "Was this standing, eating, or drinking that the doctor did? (2.74)
When a physician who lives off the sick diligently administers treatments, yet the populace falls into illness due to overeating during city festivals, processions, and weddings—
that infirmity is the fruit of the physician’s Saturn.
One who touches the secret parts of women, eats excessively, and takes away life—
truly, such a person is a physician who causes the three humors to arise in men, not a fever.
Physicians devoid of knowledge, powerful scribes,
and teachers of immoral conduct are the causes of the destruction of the subjects.
Approaching her, that villain touched her two well-knit breasts,
which were firm and constantly in contact with one another, as if they were two utterly wicked men.
She cannot endure fasting, nor is nourishing food beneficial for her pain;
let her take all kinds of food with me while we are occupied with our anxieties.
For her intellect remains dull and her constitution is unbalanced;
therefore, in this case, one should first administer curd that is both unctuous and mixed with sugar.
When Vaidyanātha had spoken thus, the astrologer and calculator, summoned with haste by the women who quickly prostrated themselves at his feet, arrived.

Salutations to that physician who knows the science of astrology and possesses the eye of knowledge; he asks whether there will be rain or no rain, while others, like fishermen of dull intellect, have lost their wits.
Though he has not even exerted himself in calculating the number of planets, lunar mansions, and stars,
he wears soiled garments as a pretext for his knowledge of the past and the future.
Within three years from now, there will be some expenditure of wealth for you;
furthermore, there will be fever, eye affliction, and even unexpected gains.
No one considers you a benefactor, and there are enemies who regard you as such; yet they have no fear of you, and the protection of their bodies is not at all hindered by you.
"You appear weak, brother; why do you not take some broth?
Surely you have jaundice; I shall drive it away with a mantra."
Thus, he who calculates the science of astrology— which is mixed with common knowledge, mantras, and medicine—
steals from those of dull intellect.
Although he already knew from public rumor the conduct of his former bride,
that rogue nevertheless drew a horoscope on a cloth of dust for no purpose at all.
When the official had scattered that heap of gold coins and flowers there,
he stood for a long time, stiff with hypocrisy, intent on counting the fingers of his own hand.
Then, repeatedly raising her eyebrows slightly, she spoke very softly:
"This woman, her face pale, is tormented by the desire for pleasure."
"The demon of passion that women harbor is difficult to restrain; thus,
I see here in this empty house that she was seized by a *guhyaka* while bathing naked, due to the union with his semen."
Thus spoke the astrologer.
Then, after the astrologer had departed and the worship of Venus had been performed, [the king] went forth,
carrying a bundle of straw and grey with dust from his feet.
With his waist bound by a rope and his gold coin-ornament shattered, the villager,
dispatched by his companion, delivered the letter to the official.
Under the pretext of sheep, ten cows were carried off on foot;
from among them, five died and five remained in the threshing floor.
Therefore, come quickly for your own liberation; even if you endure it for three days, there is profit in its absence, whereas in the village, punishment will fall upon you.
And that Brahmin who was held in captivity on account of the ghee-pipe,
he too, being without food, met his death through acute suffering.
And I delivered his formal letter of challenge to his feet; I have bound his wife and sealed his entire house.
Those whom the protector of Prāyasthāna gave me for my monthly maintenance, identifying them by their physical characteristics, were kept by me in his house.
"There is a vast heap of grain; please come here quickly. Thus was the request made with urgency on the day of Jyeṣṭhā and Ārka (Sunday).
Then the master of the kitchen, the keeper of the quivers,
his mind overflowing with joy, praised the efficiency of his assistant while reading the letter aloud.
First he was a Buddhist, then out of hypocrisy he became a Vaiṣṇava; thereafter, for the sake of protecting his wife, he developed a devotion to the Kaula scriptures.
He brought his teacher— the abode of pride, hypocrisy, and greed,
and the consecration circle for the rituals of illusion, deceit, and fickleness.
Salutations to you, O Lord Guru, who carries away wealth and wives,
who agitates all, who devours everything, and who is like a Yakṣa that consumes the night.
With a cluster of flower-like decorative patterns made of half-red lead on his forehead,
and with his great cranial dome constantly moistened by the drops and sub-drops of his abundant saliva.
With a tiny topknot tied at the very root of his ears, his earlobes marked with saffron, his eyes glassy, and his jaw large; // KNarm_2.105 //
Bald, with sparse whiskers, his speech faltering at times,
he bore a face that possessed the grace of an aged buffalo-cow.
Who can compare the thickness of the pipe-like throat of one who, in a single moment, drinks a jar of liquor amidst the clanging sounds of many jars?
Bearing a meditation belt stained with the foul odor of liquor and meat,
he had the form of a rākṣasa, his chest filled out by full breasts.
He was adorned with a deep navel-cavity filled with vermilion,
and his great belly was laden with cakes of fried dough, sweetmeats, fish, and milk-rice.
Like a turbulent cloud emitting thunderous roars of belching smoke, he released the unbearable, fresh stench of honey, meat, and indigestion.
The preceptor, his intellect blinded by the intoxication of the wine of ignorance— the most grievous of vices—
appeared like egoism personified.

Heavy in appearance, heavy in speech, heavy with indolence and stupidity, and exceedingly heavy in his genitals; likewise heavy in his mouth, beard, belly, and buttocks; heavy in deceiving courtesans, lustful women, and servants; a teacher devoid of virtuous conduct—strange indeed is this man who is heavy in every way, yet always light when it comes to the great instructions proclaimed by Śiva.
Perhaps such a person of pure conduct might be born on earth,
by whom teachers— who are repositories of impurity— have not been served.
Vying with one another to be first, they all fell at his feet;
with their heads, they created the illusion of a row of cooking pots rolling about during an earthquake.
For the protection of his wife and for the increase of his wealth,
the minister requested the venerable Guru to perform a sacrificial rite.
Having quickly written a note regarding his meager provisions with saffron,
he joyfully departed with his followers, saying, "I shall return in the morning."
The preceptor, the father-in-law— who had been diligently summoned by the official for the preparations of the sacrifice—
and then the sinful judge of the court of justice arrived.
Homage be to that preeminent teacher of the city, the possessor of enjoyments,
in whose hand the earth— with its mountains, forests, and groves— rests.
The scribe offers humble respect and speaks sweetly before [his master],
yet he does not abandon his crookedness, which resembles the horn of an old goat.
This venerable earth has been swallowed up by the court secretary, who has his ears marked with the *kalama* pen and holds birch-bark scrolls in his hands.
The Great Boar vainly made a grand display against the Daityas;
this earth was seized by the court officials, and it was not lifted up by him.
Having risen at dawn from the bed of a courtesan, reeling with wine and seeking wealth, the scribe awaits the appearance of the auspicious face [of his superior].
Surely this scribe always drinks wine at night;
otherwise, how could he wash his face with clay every single morning?
Having bathed and bearing clay, darbha grass, and sesame seeds, the scribe performs his recitation for a very long time,
contemplating forged documents, secret signs, and writing materials.
Having spat upon a Brahmin approaching before him, he quickly enters his house again and then comes out, fearing defeat.
Desiring prosperity, he pays homage on the road to what he mistakes for cow dung, only to find it is dog dung;
and desiring supernatural powers, he approaches a Caṇḍālī woman carrying her basket before him.
Surrounded by those who have arrived at the break of dawn— men with matted hair and those carrying burdens— he goes to the assembly hall, partaking of roasted meat along with a cooling drink.
Carrying a vessel well-filled with ink that was damp from being soaked in birch bark,
he seemed, by his very scent, to be foretelling one’s future dwelling in hell.
Slaying the virtuous with his ink-poisoned, wet, and curved-tusk-like pen,
the scribe acts like a sea-monster within the ocean of the assembly hall.
The drops of ink falling from his pen appear like teardrops mixed with collyrium shed by the earth as she is being plundered.
The ancestors of that man who eats the food of a divira fall headlong from their celestial palaces, wailing in the sky.
Having seen the home of his illustrious son-in-law, he was filled with joy and thought, "When, by fate, will I too have sixty daughters?"

The Āsthānadivira and the terrifying Bhūrja-bhaṭṭas were also seen there due to their association with him; they remained in his house, contemplating within themselves a future upheaval of his stationary estate.
Salutations again and again to those lords who bring about the dissolution of the worlds, including all things both stationary and moving.
Drawn by the sixfold noose and brought before the court out of fear,
the virtuous man is swallowed up by the judges, like a sacrificial offering by fish in the water.
A person who has fallen into the hands of eminent Bhaṭṭas and high-ranking ministers is released,
even if reduced to mere bones, just as one is spared by dogs intoxicated with blood.
I believe that those *brahmarākṣasas* who were not slain by Rāma because they were Brahmins and so forth are now the court poets (*āsthānabhaṭṭas*), who constantly devour human beings.
By whose word can one live— the conqueror who has been defeated, or those by whom he was defeated— when their own words have been rendered independent?
Who would not be brought to their end by those Bhaṭṭas— who were once surrounded by the guardians of hell, who have now become Vetālas, and whose hearts ring with the sound of the six case-endings?
Seeing yet blind, speaking yet mute, hearing yet deaf— the base and deceitful courtier sleeps for long, O Bhaṭṭa, unless he receives a bribe.
Eating bribes, learning the secrets of others, carving out the virtuous,
fanning up quarrels, guarding falsehoods— these are the characteristics of a Bhaṭṭa.
The brother of a leather-worker and a dancer became a dancer by association; then, knowing the ritual manuals of the *Garuḍa*, he became a protector of crops.
He too became a temple-warden for the lord of the village community— a base servant to scribes, messengers, and wheel-turners who manage peace and war.
The messenger attained the status of a Bhaṭṭa through his constant traveling back and forth between the city and the countryside;
his sons and grandsons were all twice-born officials in the court of justice.
Otherwise, how could their speech be like that of leather-workers,
who carry a very large bellows under their armpits, a vessel for storing worn-out sandals?
Thus say the judges, or those who are overly formal.
Thus ends the second jest in the *Narmamālā*.
The Third Parihāsa:
Now, at that sacrificial festival, all the clerks and their kinsmen,
as well as the adorned women, went to the house of the official.
Chalk, a golden stylus, a casket of gems containing mercury,
varieties of colored powders such as vermilion, and a thread of five colors.
Rice flour, a white umbrella, a white cloth, a canopy,
iron arrows, a razor, thread, a mirror, and a hero’s scissors.
A banner, a fan, a ritual grass-bundle, sixteen hundred thousand flowers,
two copper jars, sesame seeds, oil, and a deer-skin.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, sacrificial fuel, *darbha* grass, parched grain, white mustard seeds, clarified butter,
*bilva*, betel nut, walnuts, nutmeg, barley, and unbroken rice.
Incense, saffron, camphor, auspicious medicinal herbs, and sandalwood;
sandals, a seat, a couch, a small bell, a water-pot, and a sacrificial fire-pan.
Wine, meat, liquor, cakes, onions, fish-rice, flour-pastries, roasted juices, clear delicacies, appetizers, and sweetmeats— KNarm_3.7.
Vessels filled with sparrows, milk-rice, *kṛsarā*, and curd;
ten black and ten white goats, and fourteen rams.
In an instant, the minister Śrī, along with Bhogamitra and the other officials, prepared the bellows and all the necessary equipment, as recorded in the written list.
Then, with constant attention, the disciple fashioned a maṇḍala adorned with the female and male organs, its interior filled with vermilion.
Then the Guru, his eyes rolling from the intoxication of delighting in the Self,
was grasped by the two disciples with their left and right hands.
Followed by about a hundred disciples, he arrived slowly,
like the most fierce lord of the city himself come to commit a plunder.
A leather-worker, a butcher, a wheelwright, a fisherman, a mendicant on the market, an old courtesan, a keeper of a tavern, a drunkard, and an aged paramour.
Pañcanāraṅgaka, Rugṇa, Triṭāṅkāra, Pācaka,
Gobhakṣa, Bhairavācārya, Kulācārya, and Vāyaka.
Wearing a crest of rudrākṣa beads, carrying a water-pot, with a severed nose,
observing the great vow, having his face marked by the *bhaga*, this teacher of the Śaiva path possesses three bells.
Naked, observing the vow of silence at the shore, muttering hymns and ringing bells;
likewise, two or three women acting like madwomen, surrounded by dogs.
One smeared with excrement, one thus intoxicated, a practitioner of mantras, an alchemist,
a master of sorcery, one possessed by a creeper, a possessor of higher knowledge, and one who has realized the truth of desire.
Other servants of the teacher— the Bhaṭṭas and other rogues who attended to his drinking and dining—
entered, their faces clouded with perspiration and the fragrance of the food offerings.
Then those intoxicated men, who were destroyers of the undigested and the digested, plundering everything, being heavy and arrogant, brought about the exhaustion of sesame, incense, and ghee.
Then one, two, and many of them were likewise carried away by means of a bellows;
[along with] rice-flour, barley, walnuts, bilva fruits, arghya-offerings, ghee, and sandalwood.
Thus say the venerable teachers (*gurubhaṭṭāḥ*).
Then his own sister, a young widow (*raṇḍā*) observing her vows,
was taken by the *niyogin* for the purpose of performing the ritual service for the Guru.
Victorious is the widow with the face of a lotus, adorned with fresh youth, who steals away the splendor of the full orb of the cool-rayed moon.
A woman whose mind is shattered by a rogue who is intoxicated with pride, fierce and violent, yet a vessel of pleasure— unless he is one who has been rubbed by a fierce lover— is truly wretched.
With broad hips like a sandy bank, full thighs and breasts,
and eyes as captivating as a doe’s, this widow is an elixir for the eyes.
The widow shines with her loose hair clinging to both shoulders,
like a lotus pond filled with bees hovering over the lotus of her face and the blue-lotus eyes.
Her neck is beautiful even without a necklace, her vulva is lovely even without gold,
and the two ear-lobes of this widow are charming even without ornaments.
Deprived of flowers and betel, and having cast off her ornaments,
the widow was as if distributed by the Creator with an excess of loveliness.
Of what use is a necklace to a slender-waisted woman with beautiful hair? Of what use is a flower to her?
Of what use is collyrium to the long-eyed one? Of what use is ornamentation to a barren woman?
"What dharma is there where there is no harlot? Fie on happiness without a harlot!
May liberation never exist for us if it is devoid of a harlot!"—thus was it said by those mature libertines.
Upon seeing a young man, the harlot feigns a frown;
yet, while contemplating an embrace, she rejoices in her heart.
Remembering the pleasure of sexual union, the widow, whose thighs and breasts are full,
constantly sighs deeply as she rubs her vulva at night.
The wanton woman, full of pride, gazes askance at the handsome youth;
she flows with an abundance of semen, just as a cow yields milk.
The shaved vulva of the widow, pale and very plump,
creates the illusion of a golden slope on Mount Meru licked by the rays of the sun’s horses.
A man whose tall flagpole is stiffly raised up, brought there by means of horses and other conveyances—
whether he is capable of sexual pleasure or not— he may or may not satisfy a widow.
At the funeral rites of simple Brahmins and matted-haired ascetics, the river of passion falls under the power of those fortunate men; so does the widow.
With flowers placed upon his topknot and the sacred thread fastened around his ear,
the young Brahmin, who is fond of widows, is compared to the god of love.
To that fierce celibate student who holds his heavy staff aloft,
the widow constantly offers food for the dead with great devotion.
She always followed him on his pilgrimages,
carrying behind her a sword-blade vessel containing offerings and incense boxes.
Through their mutual longing,
that widow and that celibate student, who caused the earth to tremble at night, had their private parts thoroughly shaved.
Salutations to you who, by day, conceal your deceit while frequenting sacred bathing places;
yet at night, you are the celibate student intoxicated by drinking from the vulva of a widow.
Out of fear of the ascetics from Gauḍa and Lāṭa who wear matted hair, the harlot,
her thighs smeared with that [sandalwood paste], affectionately offers it as a garment.
Having gone to her husband’s house on a festival day, that unchaste woman,
though pretending to be virtuous, rubbed her hips with merciless seductions.
This harlot, performing initiations such as the "resurrection" of various dead men and other ascetic vows,
fearlessly offers a sacrifice of lust to those poor wretches at night.
Under the pretext of worshipping a *liṅga*, a widow places a lock on her door and uses a leather *liṅga* to scratch away her itch.
Then, as he was being attended by that fawn-eyed woman, the teacher became agitated,
and his disciples drank her in with their eyes like those oppressed by hunger drinking from a milk-yielding cow.
[Thus] the widow.
Then those men, bound by the rules of initiation,
entered with their eyes blindfolded, as if made dark by false delusion.

Then the mendicant from the marketplace, placing his knees upon the ground and joining his palms in reverence, addressed his guru, whose inner self was purified by faith, regarding the matter of the official.
O Lord, while you remain here for a very long time intent upon the sacrifice,
other disciples, eager for the festival of the rite, are waiting.
He who is renowned in the world as the greatest among householders,
having commenced the performance of sacrifices, awaits you.
Whatever countless sins there may be, such as the murder of a Brahmin and the like,
they have all been removed by you with the mere sound of a single bell ringing.
He considers all the sin of universal destruction to be as insignificant as a blade of grass,
since you have placed your hand upon his five-hooded head.
"By your grace, he has reached some indescribable state,
for even from the temples of Śaṅkara, that devotee of Śiva has seized everything."
The seizure of all one's possessions, the performance of religious duties, and the destruction of Brahmins—
whatever occurs for that [world] which is free from conceptual construction, that is indeed the manifestation of your own power.

"O Lord, this courtesan has come to invite you; she is the greatest manager of household affairs, or rather, the one who fulfills your every desire. O you who are kind to your disciples, let the water-jar be set up for her at home."
By means of the constant powders for subjugation bestowed by you,
those lovers of the wealthy have been reduced to mere skeletons.
With oaths upon her funeral pyre and her tongue and lips parched,
this woman who moves under the guise of a lover has indeed been protected for your sake.

When her wealth is exhausted, a courtesan shows a slight affection for one who has wiped away her oil with his hand upon her face, but not for one whose eyes are fixed on her; she shows parsimony toward those of diminished means, yet not toward those of the lowest castes.
If the Vaiśya woman is truly virtuous, if Time is inclined toward compassion,
and if the scribe is not a thief, then even that courtesan may be full of affection.
"O courtesan,
here has arrived this poor eye-physician who relies on everyone; by him,
with wicks made of awns of grain, the entire world has been blinded."
Since there is an abundance of eye-irritation during the summer, let this sacrifice— whose fruit is the autumn—
be performed in its entirety, with the sacrificial ground densely covered by pale creepers.
Thus ends the physician for the eyes; this barber, who subsists by extracting thorns from men, has by his skillful applications brought eggs to the size of large cooking pots.
By whom Cāmuṇḍā was formerly installed out of a desire for her head—
that very person intends to perform a sacrifice to her on the anniversary of that day.
The wise man, for the sake of joining his nose, would even cut a paste of flesh from the vulva of his own wife and give it away for a great price.
He is a surgeon;
moreover, he is an elderly merchant with a young wife and great wealth.
Due to his impotence regarding sexual intercourse, he desires an aphrodisiac.
How can an old man— his eyes streaming with mucus, gasping and coughing, and his penis flaccid and pendulous— take pleasure with a young woman?
Even when mounted in passion, an old man, his virility destroyed by the effort of rising,
finds no sleep, like a poor man brooding over a debt.
Even though his penis resembles a squeezed intestine, the old man, eager for sexual union,
places his hand upon her vulva and guards it as if it were a treasure.
Having consumed a meal of meat, milk, and ghee, an old man, driven by a desire for pleasure,
vomits it all up at night or suffers from cholera.
Seeing her husband at the honey-mixture ceremony (madhuparka) as old as a withered hide,
the young wife feels ashamed in the presence of people and sinks into the underworld.
By this aged merchant, with wealth suggested by the old lecher,
the young wife was constantly tormented as if her very organ were being cauterized.
This very man, who finds his opportunity by consuming many deposits,
is a thief during the day who makes the merchant's dwelling a field for the refuse of wealth.
During times of disease, the crooked serpent of the Kali age dances;
it sells things such as grass and wood under the names of precious substances, while they remain unrecognized for what they are.
This old man, with unblinking eyes, gazes from afar at his young, longing beloved as a sick man stares at delicious food.
Therefore, having obtained the month of Pauṣa, let it be accomplished through the perfection of mantras,
so that a passionate wife may be born from one who has attained power.
Having heard the call from his disciples, beginning with "O elder merchant," the teacher, agitated by a movement of his eyebrows, replied: "I will do everything. (KN 3.75)
Then, at the end of the day, having placed a large water-pot of Śiva before them,
those disciples drank for a long time after their meal together with the Guru.
All the wives of the officials, along with their friends and kinsmen,
vomited that leavings into skull-bowls and drank it repeatedly.
Then, one began to sing, while another wept aloud;
one reeled about, and another leaped up, making whistling sounds.
Someone, feigning extreme exhaustion born of devotion,
remains motionless for a long time as if he had reached the state of a corpse.
Someone, adorned with swaying garlands and overflowing with passion,
embraced men by the neck and even kissed women.
Then the teacher, somewhat intoxicated, sang his own poem in the vernacular of the region,
accompanied by the loud sounds of the lute and flute and the playing of the *kocchikā* drum.
Then, raising one arm out of joy with one hand,
the Guru rose slowly from his seat and danced with both hands.
Then the disciples rose up, shouting with loud laughter,
embracing women, their loincloths slipping down from their waists.
As the night slowly passed and the circle of lamps was extinguished,
their great festival of amorous play became indistinguishable from the surrounding darkness.
At dawn, the preceptor, the bestower of the water-pot, having risen with haste and being invited by other disciples, performed everything according to the prescribed rites.
The earth filled with gold belongs to physicians during times of fever and the like, to officials in the autumn season, and to teachers during the flowering season.
Then a man, a most trusted official, entered with heavy breathing, trembling as if his very sides were bursting, and glancing toward the side.
He said: "Halfway through this night, the great master of the household has departed with his followers, having taken away a vast amount of the king's wealth."
When he had departed without speaking, a certain state of flight broke out among his related officials in every single house.
Your master, his face struck by a slap, was led away in bonds by the guards;
meanwhile, that very protector was dropping excrement right before them.
Before you too are led away with your beard unshaven and bound, let this policy be adopted while the king’s terrible fear still persists.

While his friend was speaking thus, and the teacher had departed quickly accompanied by those disciples, the minister sighed and spoke in distress: iti bruvāṇe tanmitre taiḥ śiṣyaiḥ sahite gurau / tūrṇaṃ prayāte niḥśvasya niyogī duḥkhito 'vadat // KNarm_3.92 //
Alas! How great indeed is the terrible nature of the Kali age due to the wickedness of Time!
The virtuous have perished in every way; alas, Dharma has set.
Having spoken thus, as he, accompanied by his followers, was making an effort to flee, he discharged urine out of fear; at that moment, [the king] arrived, surrounded by soldiers.
Having had all his possessions confiscated by the king and having languished for a long time in prison,
he was released by his sister, the courtesan, with her wealth, and departed from there.
Then, deprived of his wealth, that reciter of mantras became a dreamer of dreams;
he bowed down to everyone, acting as a flatterer and speaking sweet words.
The official who was formerly arrogant and haughty, appearing like a religious mendicant, now acts like a bull with testicles hanging down due to the loss of his office.
It is the supreme collyrium that binds [the eyes], producing clarity of vision for those who are blinded by the intoxication of authority and are always possessed by the wrath of dogmatic views.
He who disregards even those worthy of honor when they are distressed and prostrate at his feet,
shall lose his office and must worship with his feet smeared with excrement.
Alas! In but a moment, the splendors of the scribe come into being and then cease to be, as flickering as the flames of a burning field of straw.
Then, when his wife had departed on her own initiative, that penniless man,
a nest of greed, wandered among the houses of his kinsmen seeking alms.
Within just a few days, he became coarse, emaciated, and extremely filthy, wearing tattered rags that were patched and scorched; like a *piśāca*, he became difficult to look upon.
With his buttocks, testicles, and belly scorched by the agony of being placed in a cauldron of glowing embers,
he has his knees bound with a tethering rope in order to alleviate the pain of wind-induced colic.
Having swallowed the wealth of gods and brahmins, his throat was seized by a goiter;
with his belly emaciated by hunger and his mouth parched, he wandered fallen upon the refuse heap.
With his knees and feet gnawed by dogs, with copious blood flowing profusely,
he was moved by compassion and satisfied himself with the balls of rice given as leftovers from those who eat the remnants.
With his testicles and hair still attached to a half-burnt rag hanging from him,
his head, shoulders, chest, and sides smeared with ashes, he was utterly devoid of shame.
Desiring a loincloth, he begged for it; having been given a small cake by someone, he was rejected from the drink by a woman guarding a water-station, who mistook him for a *ḍomba*.
At the onset of winter, his body was covered by the dust of a menstruating woman;
during a quarrel over begging bowls and shards,
his eyebrows, beard, and eyes were singed by the blow of a vessel containing fire.
Repeatedly struck with clubs by Caṇḍālas during funeral rites,
he lay in the mud and wailed along the main roads leading to the sacrificial grounds and holy fords.
Then that lowest of men, having fallen head-first into a sewer for human excrement with his hips thrust upward,
gave up his life.
Thus, through the penance of his wretched state, Narakaṇṭaka, while still in his physical body, reached the state of being reduced to mere bones and entered hell himself.
Thus, as the officials, scribes, and fires have gradually been stilled,
people, freed from distress and graced with contentment, rejoice.
Thus, this *Narmamālā* (Garland of Jokes) has been composed as a discussion on the wicked deeds and crooked conduct of the multitude of scribes and officials;
though fashioned for the amusement of the virtuous and for the attainment of laughter, it imparts a fruit-bearing instruction for all the world.
Thus ends the third jest in the Narmamālā.
This *Narmamālā* is completed; it is the work of Kṣemendra, whose other name was Vyāsadāsa. May there be auspiciousness!
